title: Signature Precision Ledger
description: Signature edition: every analysis records its precision configuration — which domains ran, where widening fired, which alarms were investigated and why. When a false positive is dismissed, the reasoning is logged; future runs with the same configuration inherit the dismissal with its justification. This is a Signature original method.
method: Log (domains, widening points, alarm dispositions with reasons); reuse dispositions on identical configurations; surface stale dismissals for re-review.
usage: Record dismissal reasons carefully; re-review when code or configuration changes.

demo.code:
print('alarm A12 dismissed: precision limit of intervals (reason logged)')
print('re-run, same config -> dismissal inherited with reason')

title: Signature Widening for termination
description: Signature edition: Abstract fixpoint iteration can climb forever ([0,0], [0,1], [0,2]...); widening jumps to infinity at the right moment, guaranteeing termination. It's the deliberate over-approximation that makes abstract interpretation always finish — precision traded for guaranteed answers.
method: Apply widening at loop heads after a few iterations: unstable bounds jump to +/-infinity; follow with narrowing to recover precision.
usage: Tune widening thresholds (delay widening a few iterations); always follow with a narrowing pass.

demo.code:
print('iterations: [0,0] -> [0,1] -> [0,2] -> widen -> [0,+inf]')
print('narrowing refines to [0,100] using loop condition')

title: Signature Combined domains (reduced product)
description: Signature edition: No single domain does everything: the reduced product runs several domains together, letting each refine the others (intervals tighten octagons, congruences rule out parities). Astrée's power comes from dozens of domains cooperating — combination is where industrial precision comes from.
method: Run domains in parallel; exchange information via reduction operators; iterate to a mutually-consistent fixpoint.
usage: Combine domains matching your property's needs; reductions are the engineering work that makes it pay.

demo.code:
print('intervals: x in [0,10]; congruences: x even')
print('reduced product: x in {0,2,4,6,8,10} -> proves x != 5')

title: Signature Pointer and alias analysis
description: Signature edition: Abstract interpretation tracks what pointers may point to (points-to sets, shape abstractions): 'p and q never alias' lets the analyzer — and the compiler — reason precisely about memory. Shape domains even summarize linked structures ('this is a null-terminated list'), proving memory safety structurally.
method: Abstract heap as points-to graph; transfer functions update on allocation/assignment; shape predicates summarize structures.
usage: Use for memory-safety proofs and to enable optimizations; keep the heap abstraction as coarse as the property allows.

demo.code:
print('points-to: p -> {objA}, q -> {objB}, disjoint')
print('*p = 1 cannot affect *q -> non-interference PROVED')

title: Signature Soundness: no missed bugs
description: Signature edition: Abstract interpretation's contract is soundness: the abstraction over-approximates all concrete behaviors, so 'no alarm' means 'no bug' — guaranteed. False alarms are possible (the abstraction is coarse), but missed bugs are not. That one-sided guarantee is what makes it certifiable.
method: Prove the abstract transfer functions over-approximate concrete semantics (Galois connections); then fixpoint soundness follows by construction.
usage: Trust 'clean' results absolutely; investigate alarms (some are real bugs, some are precision limits).

demo.code:
print('analysis: no alarms')
print('soundness: concrete executions ⊆ abstraction -> NO BUGS of this class, guaranteed')

title: Signature Taint analysis as abstraction
description: Signature edition: Taint tracking is abstract interpretation with a two-point domain: clean vs tainted. User input starts tainted; sanitizers clean it; sinks (SQL, shell) alarm on tainted data. Simple, fast, and the backbone of injection-vulnerability detection in industry SAST tools.
method: Two-point lattice {clean ⊑ tainted}; sources introduce taint; sanitizers lower it; sinks require clean; fixpoint over the program.
usage: Model your sanitizers accurately (the common source of false negatives); cover all sinks.

demo.code:
print('input tainted -> sanitize() -> clean -> SQL sink: OK')
print('input tainted -> SQL sink directly: ALARM (injection risk)')

title: Signature Astrée industrial analyzer
description: Signature edition: Astrée proved the absence of runtime errors in Airbus flight-control software — 132,000 lines of C, zero false alarms on the target property class. It combines dozens of domains (intervals, octagons, decision trees) with trace partitioning: abstract interpretation at industrial scale, certifying real aircraft.
method: Layer specialized domains; partition traces by control-flow history; iterate to fixpoint; zero-alarm configuration per codebase.
usage: Specialize the domain combination per codebase; achieving zero alarms takes tuning but pays off in certification.

print('Astrée on flight control: 132,000 lines')
print('result: no division by zero, no overflow, no invalid array access — PROVED')

title: Signature Octagon domain (relational)
description: Signature edition: Intervals can't express relationships ('x < y'); the octagon domain tracks constraints of the form ±x ±y ≤ c, capturing exactly those relations with reasonable cost. It proves array-bounds and ordering properties that non-relational domains miss — the sweet spot for many real analyses.
method: Represent constraints as a difference-bound matrix; closure via Floyd-Warshall; join/meet on the matrix; widening on unstable bounds.
usage: Use when relations between variables matter (indices, counters); watch the cubic cost on many variables.

demo.code:
print('tracked: x - y <= 0 (i.e., x <= y)')
print('array access a[y] with y < len and x <= y -> a[x] safe: PROVED')

title: Signature Polyhedra domain (Cousot-Halbwachs)
description: Signature edition: The most precise common numeric domain: convex polyhedra capture arbitrary linear relations (2x + 3y ≤ 7). It proves what octagons can't, at higher cost — the precision end of the tradeoff curve, used when the property demands full linear reasoning.
method: Polyhedra as constraint sets; operations via linear programming (double description); widening on constraint sets.
usage: Reserve for small critical kernels where linear relations are essential; expect high cost.

demo.code:
print('tracked: 2x + 3y <= 7')
print('property needs 2x+3y bound -> polyhedra proves it, octagon cannot')
